text:
Build a blog API in Go in 15 minutes.
Posts, comments, validation, and tests — with kanna.
Start with a Post: title, body, ID, and timestamps.

Declare the database operations as a Go interface.
kanna-orm generates the PostgreSQL implementation.

kanna-orm supports PostgreSQL and MySQL.
This demo uses PostgreSQL.

Get, list, insert, update, delete.
The interface describes what the app needs.

Inspect the generated code: ordinary Go and SQL.
kanna-orm writes the creation and update times.

Require a title and limit its length.
kanna-validator generates checks without reflection.

Keep the JSON response separate from the model.
kanna-mapper generates the field mapping.

Declare the API's dependencies.
kanna-di will generate the constructor.
Route HTTP requests with Go's standard library.

Decode and validate the request, insert the post,
then map the result to a JSON response.
Use a generated scope to list posts by creation time.

Update the post and return it as stored.
kanna-orm keeps its creation time.

Generate the constructor.
The dependency wiring is plain Go.

Open the PostgreSQL pool and start the HTTP server.
Keep main small.
The first post is live. HTTP 201 Created.

An empty title returns HTTP 422
with a field-specific validation error.

Now add comments to the working blog.
A foreign key links each comment to a post.

Declare the comment operations.
Generate the database code again as the app grows.

Extend the response with comments.
The mapper will generate the nested conversion.
Validate the comment, then insert it for an existing post.

Load the post with its comments
and return the nested JSON response.
Add one dependency, one route, and WithComments().
Regenerate SQL, validation, mapping, and dependency wiring.
Generate fixtures and test against real PostgreSQL.

Run the test in a transaction
and roll it back when the test ends.
Insert a generated fixture, update it, and query it back.

Generate a comment fixture linked to the post.
Check that eager loading returns the relation.
Verify the nested response mapping too.

Delete the post and check that its comments are gone.
PostgreSQL enforces ON DELETE CASCADE.
Tests pass. Check that every generated file is up to date.

Post a comment. The API returns the post
with its comments in one JSON response.

Posts, comments, validation, mapping, DI, and fixtures.
A working blog API — in under 15 minutes.
